sections.semantic_excerpt: C.2 Tensor Programming Primitives A shape mismatch crash, a silently wrong broadcast, a kernel running at 5 percent of peak because of a noncontiguous tensor—these common ML engineering failures all trace back to the same layer of abstraction. Tensor programming translates the abstract math of linear algebra into concrete array manipulations that run on hardware. C.2.1 Computational complexity cheat sheet Table C.1 provides a quantitative reference for the most common building blocks.

sections.title: Mechanics of Learning
sections.semantic_excerpt: C.3 Mechanics of Learning Valid tensor programs make training loops possible. Backpropagation orchestrates these tensors to compute gradients, transforming a forward prediction into a backward learning signal. Systems Perspective C.2: Why this matters When training fails—loss goes to NaN, gradients explode, or memory runs out—understanding what backpropagation actually does is essential for diagnosing the problem.

sections.title: Baur–Strassen Reverse-Mode AD Complexity Theorem
sections.semantic_excerpt: C.4 Baur–Strassen Reverse-Mode AD Complexity Theorem Modern deep learning scales to hundreds of billions of parameters because evaluating the full gradient vector ∇f(x) of a scalar loss function f∶RN→Rrequires compute proportional to evaluating f(x) itself, with a constant-factor bound independent of the input dimension N. Baur and Strassen proved this complexity result in 1983.

sections.title: FlashAttention Tiling & Online Softmax Recurrence Proof
sections.semantic_excerpt: C.5 FlashAttention Tiling & Online Softmax Recurrence Proof Standard self-attention in transformers requires materializing an N× Nattention score matrix in HBM, creating an O(N2) memory bandwidth bottleneck. FlashAttention eliminates this bottleneck by tiling query, key, and value matrices and recomputing attention using an online softmax recurrence without materializing intermediate scores to HBM.

sections.title: Kaplan & Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Scaling Law Derivation
sections.semantic_excerpt: C.6 Kaplan & Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Scaling Law Derivation Determining the compute-optimal allocation between model parameters Nand training dataset tokens Dfor a given floating-point budget Cis a central decision in large language model system design. This section provides the rigorous mathematical derivation of compute-optimal scaling laws using Lagrange multipliers, contrasting the original findings of Kaplan et al. with the compute-optimal corrections of Hoffmann et al..

sections.title: Physics of Computing
sections.semantic_excerpt: D.2 Physics of Computing Raw hardware specs—TFLOP/s, TB/s, watt budgets—are necessary but insufficient for performance reasoning. Without compact analytical models, an engineer cannot distinguish a compute-bound workload from a memory-bound one, or predict whether doubling GPUs will halve training time. The models in this section turn those distinctions into quantitative checks.

sections.title: Computer Architecture Essentials
sections.semantic_excerpt: D.3 Computer Architecture Essentials A GPU advertises 1,000 TFLOP/s, yet a kernel achieves only 30 TFLOP/s. The gap may reflect data movement, insufficient parallelism, synchronization, launch overhead, or software inefficiency. While physics sets theoretical performance bounds, computer architecture defines the machinery that determines how close a real workload can get.

concepts.definition: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, a transformer-based language model introduced by Google in 2018 that revolutionized natural language processing through masked language modeling pretraining.

concepts.name: BF16

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A 16-bit floating-point format developed by Google Brain that maintains the same dynamic range as FP32 but with reduced precision, making it particularly suitable for deep learning training.

concepts.name: bias

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A learnable parameter added to the weighted sum in each neuron that shifts the activation function, allowing neurons to activate even when all inputs are zero and providing additional flexibility for the network to fit complex patterns.

concepts.name: binarization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: An extreme quantization technique that reduces neural network weights, activations, or both to binary values (typically -1 and +1), achieving maximum compression but often requiring specialized training procedures and hardware support.

concepts.name: biological neuron

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A cell in the nervous system that receives, processes, and transmits information through electrical and chemical signals, serving as inspiration for artificial neural networks.

concepts.name: bitter lesson

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: Richard Sutton’s 2019 observation that general methods using computation consistently outperform approaches encoding human expertise, suggesting that systems engineering enabling computational scale is central to AI advancement.

concepts.name: black box

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A system whose inputs and outputs are observable but whose internal workings are inaccessible or opaque. This opacity is particularly problematic when the system makes consequential decisions without explaining its reasoning.

concepts.name: BLAS

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms, a specification for low-level routines that perform common linear algebra operations such as vector addition, scalar multiplication, dot products, and matrix operations, forming the computational foundation of modern ML frameworks.

concepts.name: block sparse matrix

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A sparse matrix whose nonzero values appear in dense blocks rather than isolated elements, preserving structure that hardware kernels can exploit efficiently.

concepts.name: blue-green deployment

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A deployment strategy using two production environments so traffic can switch to a validated new version while the old version remains available for rollback.

concepts.name: bounding box

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A rectangular annotation that identifies object locations in images by drawing a box around each object of interest, commonly used in computer vision training datasets.

concepts.name: brittleness

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: The tendency of rule-based AI systems to fail completely when encountering inputs that fall outside their programmed scenarios, no matter how similar those inputs might be to what they were designed to handle.

concepts.name: caching

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A technique for storing frequently accessed data in high-speed storage systems to

concepts.name: caching allocator

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A framework memory manager that reuses device-memory blocks instead of calling the hardware allocator for every tensor, reducing allocation latency and fragmentation.

concepts.name: calibration

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: The process in post-training quantization of analyzing a representative dataset to determine optimal quantization parameters, including scale factors and zero points, that minimize accuracy loss when converting from high to low precision.

concepts.name: canary deployment

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A deployment strategy where new model versions receive a small percentage of production traffic to validate behavior before full rollout, enabling early detection of issues with minimal user impact.

concepts.name: CAP theorem

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A distributed systems principle stating that, during a network partition, a data store cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability for every request.

concepts.name: carbon footprint

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: The total greenhouse gas emissions, typically measured in CO2 equivalent, produced directly and indirectly by training and operating an ML system.

concepts.name: carbon intensity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: The emissions produced per unit of energy, usually measured as kg CO2e per kWh, used to convert ML energy use into carbon impact.

concepts.name: Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: In the CS-2 generation, a single-wafer processor containing 2.6 trillion transistors and 850,000 cores, designed to eliminate inter-device communication bottlenecks in large-scale machine learning training.

concepts.name: chain rule

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: The calculus rule enabling computation of derivatives for composite functions, fundamental to backpropagation.

concepts.name: channelwise quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A quantization granularity approach where each channel in a layer uses its own set of quantization parameters, providing more precise representation than layerwise quantization while maintaining hardware efficiency.

concepts.name: CI/CD pipelines

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery automated workflows that streamline model development by integrating testing, validation, and deployment processes.

concepts.name: circuit breaker pattern

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A resilience pattern that stops or redirects calls to an unhealthy service after repeated failures to prevent cascading failure and enable fallback behavior.

concepts.name: classification labels

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: Simple categorical annotations that assign specific tags or categories to data examples, representing the most basic form of supervised learning annotation.

concepts.name: Cloud ML

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 76; printed p. 51

concepts.definition: Cloud machine learning is the deployment paradigm that trades latency for elastic compute by locating ML workloads in centralized data centers, decoupling computational capacity from the physical location of data sources and users. 1. Significance: Cloud deployment dominates the Rpeak term: a single cloud region can provision thousands of accelerators on demand, delivering aggregate throughput that no typical on-premise installation can match economically...

concepts.name: CloudSuite

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: Benchmark suite developed at EPFL that addresses modern data center workloads including web search, data analytics, and media streaming, measuring end-to-end performance across network, storage, and compute dimensions.

concepts.name: Cold start

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 723; printed p. 708

concepts.definition: Cold start is the initialization latency incurred when instantiating a new model replica. Significance: It represents the fixed cost of state hydration (loading weights, compiling graphs), which can take seconds or minutes, effectively blocking the system’s ability to scale elastically in response to traffic bursts.

concepts.name: cold-start performance

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: Time required for a system to transition from idle state to active execution, particularly important in serverless environments where models are loaded on demand.

concepts.name: collaborative filtering

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: A technique used in recommendation systems that predicts user preferences by identifying patterns in interactions from many users, using the collective behavior of the crowd rather than just item properties.

concepts.name: communication tax

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 922; printed p. 912

concepts.definition: The performance penalty incurred in distributed systems due to the latency and bandwidth costs of synchronizing state between nodes.

concepts.name: compound AI systems

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: AI architectures that combine multiple specialized models and components working together, rather than relying on a single monolithic model, enabling modularity, specialization, and improved interpretability.

concepts.name: compressed sparse row (CSR)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A memoryefficient storage format for sparse matrices that uses three arrays (values, column indices, row pointers) to store only nonzero elements, reducing memory from O(N2) (for an N×Nmatrix) to O(K+ N) where Kis the number of nonzeros.

concepts.name: computational graph

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A directed graph representing the sequence of operations in neural network computation, enabling automatic differentiation.

concepts.name: computer engineering

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: An engineering discipline that emerged in the late 1960s to address the growing complexity of integrating hardware and software systems, combining expertise from electrical engineering and computer science to design and build complex computing systems.

concepts.name: computing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A distributed computing

concepts.name: concept drift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The phenomenon where P(Y∣ X), the statistical relationship between inputs and targets, changes over time, distinct from data drift in P(X); this can, but need not, degrade a fixed model’s performance. Detecting it typically requires outcome labels because input drift alone does not establish a conditional change.

concepts.name: conditional computation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A dynamic optimization technique where different parts of a neural network are selectively activated based on input characteristics, reducing computational load by skipping unnecessary computations for specific inputs.

concepts.name: consensus labeling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A quality control approach that collects multiple annotations for the same data point to identify controversial cases and improve label reliability through inter-annotator agreement.

concepts.name: containerization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: Packaging applications and their dependencies into portable, isolated containers using tools like Docker to ensure consistent execution across different environments.

concepts.name: continuous batching

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: An LLM serving technique that adds and removes requests from an inference batch between token-generation steps as sequences start and finish.

concepts.name: continuous integration

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A software development practice where code changes are automatically integrated, tested, and validated multiple times per day to detect issues early in the development cycle.

concepts.name: convolution

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A mathematical operation that slides a filter (kernel) across input data to extract features such as edges, textures, or patterns. Convolution is fundamental to convolutional neural networks and particularly effective for processing images and spatial data.

concepts.name: convolutional neural network

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A specialized neural network architecture designed for processing grid-like data such as images, using convolutional layers that apply filters to detect local features.

concepts.name: Convolutional neural networks

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 258; printed p. 236

concepts.definition: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are architectures that exploit translation equivariance and spatial locality to share learned filters across all spatial positions, decoupling parameter count from input resolution. Significance: Weight sharing produces dramatic parameter reduction.

concepts.name: coreset

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A small subset of a dataset selected to preserve important statistical or training properties of the full dataset while reducing training or evaluation cost.

concepts.name: correction cascade

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: An ML technical-debt pattern where fixing one component creates new failures or redesign needs elsewhere because data and model dependencies propagate through the system.

concepts.name: covariate shift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A distribution shift where input feature distributions change while the relationship between features and labels remains stable.

concepts.name: CP decomposition

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition that expresses a tensor as a sum of rank-one components, used to compress neural network layers by reducing the number of parameters while preserving computational functionality.

concepts.name: credit assignment problem

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The challenge of determining which weights in a multi-layer network contributed to prediction errors.

concepts.name: CRISP-DM

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining, a structured methodology developed in 1996 that defines six phases for data projects: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, and deployment.

concepts.name: critical batch size

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The batch size beyond which larger batches provide diminishing optimization benefit and may reduce generalization, limiting simple linear learning-rate scaling.

concepts.name: cross-entropy loss

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A loss function commonly used in classification tasks that measures the difference between predicted probability distributions and true class labels, providing strong gradients for effective learning.

concepts.name: crowdsourcing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A collaborative data collection approach that uses distributed individuals via the internet to perform annotation tasks, enabling scalable dataset creation through platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk.

concepts.name: cuBLAS

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: NVIDIA’s CUDA Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms library that provides GPU-accelerated implementations of standard linear algebra operations, enabling high-performance matrix computations on NVIDIA graphics processing units.

concepts.name: CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: NVIDIA’s parallel computing platform and programming model that enables generalpurpose computing on graphics processing units (GPUs), allowing machine learning frameworks to use massive parallelism for accelerated tensor operations.

concepts.name: CUDA stream

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: An ordered queue of GPU work used to schedule kernels, memory transfers, and synchronization events so independent operations can overlap.

concepts.name: Dartmouth conference

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The legendary 8-week workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956 where AI was officially born, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon, following their 1955 proposal, which introduced the term artificial intelligence.

concepts.name: data as source code

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The Software 2.0 principle that training data defines ML system behavior, so dataset changes act like behaviorchanging code changes.

concepts.name: data augmentation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The process of artificially expanding training datasets by creating modified versions of existing data through transformations like rotation, scaling, or noise injection.

concepts.name: Data cascade

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 137; printed p. 112

concepts.definition: Data cascade is an ML systems failure mode in which upstream data quality problems propagate through collection, labeling, feature engineering, training, evaluation, and deployment, amplifying into downstream model failures or user harm. 1...

concepts.name: data cascades

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: Systemic failures where data quality issues compound over time, creating downstream negative consequences such as model failures, costly rebuilding, or project termination.

concepts.name: data center

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A facility that houses computer systems and associated components such as telecommunications and storage systems,

concepts.name: data contracts

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: Explicit agreements between data producers and consumers defining schema, quality expectations, and service levels to prevent downstream breakage.

concepts.name: data curation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The process of selecting, organizing, and maintaining high-quality datasets by removing irrelevant information, correcting errors, and ensuring data meets specific standards for machine learning applications.

concepts.name: data debt

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: Accumulated data quality, documentation, schema, lineage, or freshness liabilities that compound over time and degrade model behavior.

concepts.name: data drift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The phenomenon where the input distribution P(X) changes over time even though code remains unchanged; this may affect model performance but does not guarantee degradation. It can be monitored without labels, although labels are needed to measure its effect on quality.

concepts.name: data echoing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A training input-pipeline technique that reuses batches, often with fresh augmentation, when data preparation is slower than accelerator consumption.

concepts.name: Data engineering

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 133; printed p. 108

concepts.definition: Data engineering is the infrastructure layer that manages the lifecycle of data from source to model, encompassing acquisition, transformation, storage, and governance. Significance: Its critical function is ensuring training-serving consistency, preventing silent degradation by decoupling the model from the volatility of raw data.

concepts.name: data governance

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The framework of policies, procedures, and technologies that ensure data security, privacy, compliance, and ethical use throughout the machine learning pipeline.

concepts.name: data gravity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The architectural pull created by large data volumes, transfer time, bandwidth limits, and egress cost, which tends to draw computation toward the data.

concepts.name: data ingestion

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The process of collecting and importing raw data from various sources into a system where it can be stored, processed, and prepared for machine learning applications.

concepts.name: data lake

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A storage repository that holds structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data in its native format, using schema-onread approaches for flexible data analysis.

concepts.name: data lakehouse

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A storage architecture that combines data lake flexibility with warehousestyle query semantics, schema management, and transactional guarantees.

concepts.name: data lineage

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The documentation and tracking of data flow through various transformations and processes, providing visibility into data origins and modifications for compliance and debugging.

concepts.name: data locality

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The principle that data and computation should be colocated when transfer latency, bandwidth, or cost dominates remote processing.

concepts.name: data parallelism

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A distributed training strategy that splits the dataset across multiple devices while each device maintains a complete copy of the model, enabling parallel computation of gradients.

concepts.name: data pipeline

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The infrastructure and workflows that automate the movement and transformation of data from sources through processing stages to final storage or consumption.

concepts.name: data quality

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: The degree to which data meets requirements for accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness, directly impacting machine learning model performance.

concepts.name: data quality multiplier

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The idea that improvements in data quality can amplify gains from model and system changes because all downstream stages depend on the data.

concepts.name: Data selection

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 442; printed p. 424

concepts.definition: Data selection is the process of maximizing the information-compute ratio (ICR) of a training dataset. Significance: It identifies data worth retaining, prioritizing, or generating for the target objective, reducing the total operations (O) when redundant or noisy samples can be excluded without losing required coverage.

concepts.name: data validation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The systematic verification that collected data meets quality standards, is properly formatted, and contains accurate information suitable for machine learning model training and evaluation.

concepts.name: data versioning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The practice of tracking and managing different versions of datasets over time, similar to code versioning, to ensure reproducibility and enable rollback to previous data states when needed.

concepts.name: data warehouse

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A centralized repository optimized for analytical queries (OLAP) that stores integrated, structured data from multiple sources in a standardized schema.

concepts.name: data-centric approach

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A machine learning paradigm that prioritizes improving data quality, diversity, and curation rather than solely focusing on model architecture improvements to achieve better performance.

concepts.name: data-centric computing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: Systems optimized for the efficient ingestion of data and iterative refinement of model parameters, where the programmer’s job is to curate data.

concepts.name: dataflow architecture

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Specialized computing architecture where instruction execution is determined by data availability rather than a program counter, enabling highly parallel processing of neural network operations.

concepts.name: dataflow challenges

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Technical difficulties in managing data movement and dependencies in hardware accelerators, including memory bandwidth limitations and synchronization requirements.

concepts.name: datasheets for datasets

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Documentation for training data that captures provenance, collection methodology, demographic composition, and known limitations affecting model behavior.

concepts.name: dead letter queue

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A separate storage mechanism for data that fails processing, allowing for later analysis and potential reprocessing of problematic data without blocking the main pipeline.

concepts.name: deduplication

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The removal of exact, nearduplicate, or semantically redundant samples from a dataset to reduce storage, training compute, and leakage risk.

concepts.name: deep learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A subfield of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with multiple layers to automatically learn hierarchical representations from data without explicit feature engineering.

concepts.name: demographic parity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A fairness criterion requiring that the probability of receiving a positive prediction is independent of group membership across protected attributes.

concepts.name: Dennard scaling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The observation that as transistors became smaller, their power density remained constant, enabling higher performance at the same power envelope. Its breakdown around 2005 ended the era of free frequency scaling.

concepts.name: dense layer

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A fully-connected neural network layer where each neuron receives input from all neurons in the previous layer, enabling comprehensive information integration across features.

concepts.name: deployment constraints

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Operational limitations such as hardware resources, network connectivity, regulatory requirements, and integration requirements that influence how machine learning models are implemented in production environments.

concepts.name: deployment paradigm

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A distinct approach to hosting and executing ML models characterized by specific resource constraints and operational properties, such as Cloud ML, Edge ML, Mobile ML, or TinyML.

concepts.name: depthwise separable convolution

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A convolution factorization that applies spatial filtering independently per channel and then mixes channels with a pointwise convolution to reduce computation.

concepts.name: DevOps

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Software development practice that combines development and operations teams to shorten development cycles and

concepts.name: Dhrystone

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Integer-based benchmark introduced in 1984 that measures integer and string operations in DMIPS (Dhrystone MIPS), designed to complement floatingpoint benchmarks with typical programming constructs.

concepts.name: diabetic retinopathy

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A diabetes complication that damages blood vessels in the retina, serving as a leading cause of preventable blindness and a key application area for medical AI screening systems.

concepts.name: differential privacy

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A mathematical framework for quantifying and limiting privacy loss when releasing statistical information about datasets by bounding how much the output distribution can change when any one individual’s data is added or removed.

concepts.name: direct memory access (DMA)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A mechanism that lets a device move data to or from memory without CPU-managed copying for each transfer, enabling overlap and reducing host overhead.

concepts.name: disaggregated evaluation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The practice of breaking down model performance metrics by demographic groups or other factors to reveal disparities that are hidden by aggregate measures.

concepts.name: dispatch tax

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Runtime overhead from launching and orchestrating many small operations through the host framework instead of executing fused or compiled graph regions.

concepts.name: distributed computing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: An approach that processes data across multiple machines or processors simultaneously, enabling scalable handling of large datasets through frameworks like Apache Spark.

concepts.name: distributed intelligence

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The placement of computational capabilities across multiple devices and locations rather than relying on a single centralized system, enabling local processing and decision-making.

concepts.name: distributed training

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A method of training machine learning models across multiple machines or devices to handle larger datasets and models that exceed single-device computational or memory capacity.

concepts.name: distribution shift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A change in the statistical properties of data between training and deployment, or over time during deployment. Types include covariate shift (input distribution changes), label shift (output distribution changes), and concept drift (relationship between inputs and outputs changes).

concepts.name: DLRM

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Deep Learning Recommendation Model, an architecture developed by Meta that combines categorical embeddings with a bottom multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and top MLP to handle the massive scale and sparsity of recommendation system workloads.

concepts.name: domain-specific architecture

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Hardware designs tailored to optimize specific computational workloads, trading flexibility for improved performance and energy efficiency compared to general-purpose processors.

concepts.name: dropout

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A regularization technique that randomly sets a fraction of input units to zero during training to prevent overfitting and improve generalization.

concepts.name: dying ReLU problem

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A failure mode where ReLU neurons become permanently inactive and output zero for all inputs, preventing them from contributing to learning when weighted inputs consistently produce negative preactivations.

concepts.name: dynamic batching

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A serving technique that waits briefly to group independent requests into a batch, improving throughput while adding controlled batch-formation latency.

concepts.name: dynamic graph

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A computational graph that is built and modified during program execution, allowing for flexible model architectures and easier debugging but potentially limiting optimization opportunities compared to static graphs.

concepts.name: dynamic pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A pruning approach that changes which parameters or units are inactive in response to input data or training dynamics, rather than relying only on a fixed pruning decision.

concepts.name: dynamic quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: The process of storing neural-network weights at lower precision and determining activation quantization parameters at runtime, reducing memory use while requiring supported low-precision kernels for speedup.

concepts.name: dynamic random-access memory (DRAM)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A type of volatile memory that stores data in capacitors and requires periodic refresh cycles, commonly used as main memory in computer systems.

concepts.name: dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Power management technique that adjusts processor voltage and clock frequency based on workload demands to optimize energy consumption while maintaining performance.

concepts.name: D·A·M taxonomy

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 923; printed p. 913

concepts.definition: A diagnostic framework that analyzes ML system bottlenecks through three interacting axes: Data (information flow, bounded by bandwidth), Algorithm (mathematical logic, bounded by total operations), and Machine (physical execution, bounded by peak throughput).

concepts.name: eager execution

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: An execution mode where operations are evaluated immediately as they are called in the code, providing intuitive debugging and development experience but potentially sacrificing some optimization opportunities available in graph-based execution.

concepts.name: early exit architectures

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Neural network designs that include multiple prediction heads at different depths, allowing samples to exit early when confident predictions can be made, reducing average computational cost per inference.

concepts.name: edge

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: paradigm that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, reducing latency and bandwidth usage.

concepts.name: edge deployment

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: A deployment strategy where machine learning models run locally on devices at the network edge rather than in centralized cloud servers, reducing latency and enabling operation without constant internet connectivity.

concepts.name: Edge ML

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 81; printed p. 56

concepts.definition: Edge machine learning is the deployment paradigm optimized for latency determinism and data locality by locating computation physically adjacent to data sources. Significance: It circumvents the distance penalty (Llat) of the cloud, trading elastic scale for a fixed local compute capacity (Rpeak).

concepts.name: efficiency frontier

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: efficiency frontier The optimal trade-off curve between accuracy and computational cost (latency, energy, or memory), where no model exists that is both more accurate and more efficient.

concepts.name: EfficientNet

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: EfficientNet A family of neural network architectures discovered through neural architecture search that achieves better accuracyefficiency trade-offs by using compound scaling to balance network depth, width, and input resolution.

concepts.name: ELIZA

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: One of the first chatbots created by MIT’s Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966 that could simulate human conversation through pattern matching and substitution, notable because people began forming emotional attachments to this simple program.

concepts.name: embedded systems

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 924; printed p. 914

concepts.definition: Computer systems with dedicated functions within larger mechanical or electrical systems, typically designed for specific tasks with real-time computing constraints.

concepts.name: embedding sharding

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Splitting large embedding tables across devices or nodes so they fit in aggregate memory, while adding communication to gather embeddings for each batch.

concepts.name: embedding table

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A lookup table that maps discrete IDs or tokens to dense vectors, often dominating memory in recommendation models and large vocabularies.

concepts.name: emergent behaviors

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Unexpected system-wide patterns or characteristics that arise from the interaction of individual components, often becoming apparent only when systems operate at scale or in real-world conditions.

concepts.name: encoder-decoder

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: An architectural pattern where an encoder processes input into an intermediate representation and a decoder generates output from this representation, commonly used in sequence-to-sequence tasks.

concepts.name: end-to-end benchmarks

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Comprehensive evaluation methodology that assesses entire AI system pipelines including data processing, model execution, postprocessing, and infrastructure components.

concepts.name: energy efficiency

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: energy efficiency The measure of computational work performed per unit of energy consumed, typically expressed as operations per joule and crucial for battery-powered and data center deployments.

concepts.name: energy per inference

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The total energy consumed to produce one model prediction, including model execution and relevant system overhead.

concepts.name: epoch

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: One complete pass through the entire training dataset during neural network training, consisting of multiple batch iterations depending on dataset size and batch size.

concepts.name: equal opportunity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A fairness criterion requiring equal true positive rates across different demographic groups.

concepts.name: equalized odds

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A fairness criterion requiring that both true positive and false positive rates are equal across different demographic groups.

concepts.name: expected calibration error (ECE)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A metric measuring the gap between predicted confidence and observed accuracy across confidence bins, used to assess probability calibration.

concepts.name: experiment tracking

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The systematic recording and management of machine learning experiments, including hyperparameters, model versions, training data, and performance metrics, to enable comparison and reproducibility.

concepts.name: expert systems

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: AI systems first developed in the mid-1960s that captured human expert knowledge in specific domains, exemplified by MYCIN for diagnosing blood infections, representing a shift from general AI to domain-specific applications.

concepts.name: extract, load, transform (ELT)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A data processing paradigm that first loads raw data into the target system before applying transformations, providing flexibility for evolving analytical needs.

concepts.name: extract, transform, load (ETL)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A traditional data processing paradigm that transforms data before loading it into a data warehouse, resulting in ready-to-query formatted data.

concepts.name: fairness laundering

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A failure mode where removing explicit protected attributes makes a system appear compliant while correlated proxy variables still reproduce discriminatory outcomes.

concepts.name: false positive rate (FPR)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The proportion of actual negative cases incorrectly classified as positive, computed as false positives divided by false positives plus true negatives.

concepts.name: FarmBeats

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A Microsoft Research project that applies machine learning and IoT technologies to agriculture, using edge computing to collect real-time data on soil conditions and crop health while demonstrating distributed AI systems in challenging real-world environments.

concepts.name: feature engineering

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The process of manually designing and extracting relevant features from raw data to improve machine learning model performance, largely automated in deep learning systems.

concepts.name: feature map

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The output of a convolutional layer representing the response of learned filters to different spatial locations in the input, capturing detected features at various positions.

concepts.name: feature store

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A specialized data storage system that provides standardized, reusable features for machine learning, enabling feature sharing across multiple models and teams.

concepts.name: federated learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A machine learning approach that trains algorithms across decentralized edge devices or servers holding local data samples, without exchanging the raw data.

concepts.name: feedback loop

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A cyclical process where outputs influence future inputs. In ML, this includes both beneficial cycles (where model outputs inform system improvement) and harmful ones (where a model’s predictions influence its own future training data, potentially reinforcing and amplifying initial biases over time).

concepts.name: feedforward network

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A neural network architecture where information flows in one direction from input to output layers without cycles, forming the foundation for many deep learning models.

concepts.name: field-programmable gate array (FPGA)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A reconfigurable integrated circuit that can be programmed after manufacturing to implement custom digital circuits and specialized computations, offering flexibility between general-purpose processors and ASICs.

concepts.name: fine-tuning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Adapting a pretrained model to a target task or domain by continuing training on task-specific data.

concepts.name: Five-Pillar Framework

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: An organizational structure for ML systems engineering comprising five interconnected disciplines: Data Engineering, Training Systems, Deployment Infrastructure, Operations and Monitoring, and Ethics and Governance.

concepts.name: FlashAttention

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: An IO-aware attention algorithm that tiles computation to avoid materializing the full attention matrix in highbandwidth memory, reducing memory traffic and enabling longer sequences.

concepts.name: floating-point unit (FPU)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A specialized processor component designed to perform arithmetic operations on floating-point numbers with high precision and efficiency.

concepts.name: FLOP/s

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Floating-Point Operations per Second, a measure of computational throughput that quantifies the number of floating-point operations a system can perform per second.

concepts.name: forgetting events

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Events where a model changes from classifying an example correctly to misclassifying it later in training, marking difficult or informative samples.

concepts.name: forward pass

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The process of computing neural network predictions by passing input data through successive layers, applying weights, biases, and activation functions at each stage to produce outputs. Also called forward propagation.

concepts.name: foundation model

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: Large-scale machine learning models trained on broad data that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks, serving as a base for specialized applications.

concepts.name: four pillars framework

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A data engineering framework organizing concerns into Quality, Reliability, Scalability, and Governance to manage the data lifecycle.

concepts.name: FP16

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: 16-bit floating-point numerical representation that reduces memory usage and accelerates computation on modern hardware accelerators while maintaining acceptable precision for many machine learning applications.

concepts.name: FP32

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: 32-bit floating-point numerical representation that provides standard precision for mathematical computations but requires more memory and computational resources than lower-precision formats.

concepts.name: FP32 to INT8

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A common quantization transformation that converts 32-bit floating-point weights and activations to 8-bit integers, achieving roughly 4× memory reduction while maintaining acceptable accuracy for many models.

concepts.name: FP8

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: An 8-bit floating-point format family used on newer accelerators for high-throughput training and inference, requiring careful scaling because of limited precision and range.

concepts.name: framework

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: breakdown of neural network frameworks into hardware-mappable components, enabling efficient distribution of operations across processing elements.

concepts.name: GEMM

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: General Matrix Multiply operations that follow the pattern C= αAB+βC, representing the fundamental computational kernel underlying most neural network operations including fully connected layers and convolutional layers.

concepts.name: GEMV

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: General Matrix-Vector multiplication operations that compute the product of a matrix and a vector, commonly used in neural network computations and requiring careful optimization for memory access patterns.

concepts.name: generalization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The ability of a machine learning model to perform well on unseen data that differs from the training set, often improved through diverse and high-quality training data.

concepts.name: generalization gap

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The difference between a model’s performance on training data and its performance on held-out data. A large generalization gap can indicate overfitting to the training data.

concepts.name: generative AI

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A category of artificial intelligence systems capable of creating new content such as text, images, audio, or video based on learned patterns from training data.

concepts.name: Goodhart’s Law

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: The observation that when a measure becomes an optimization target, it can stop representing the underlying goal.

concepts.name: GPT-2

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A 1.5-billion parameter autoregressive language model released by OpenAI in 2019, serving as a primary lighthouse model for analyzing memory bandwidth constraints in transformer inference.

concepts.name: graceful degradation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A system design principle where services continue functioning with reduced capabilities when faced with partial failures or data unavailability.

concepts.name: gradient accumulation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A technique that simulates larger batch sizes by accumulating gradients from multiple smaller batches before updating model parameters, enabling training with limited memory.

concepts.name: gradient clipping

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: An optimization technique that mitigates exploding gradients by limiting their magnitude during backpropagation, typically by scaling gradients when their norm exceeds a threshold.

concepts.name: gradient compression

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A technique used in distributed training to reduce the communication overhead by compressing gradient information exchanged between computing nodes.

concepts.name: gradient descent

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts neural network parameters in the direction that minimizes the loss function, using gradients to determine update directions and magnitudes.

concepts.name: gradient synchronization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The process in distributed training where locally computed gradients are aggregated across devices to ensure all devices update their parameters consistently.

concepts.name: gradient-based pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 925; printed p. 915

concepts.definition: A pruning method that uses gradient information to rank param-

concepts.name: GraNd (Gradient Normed)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A data selection score based on the norm of an example’s gradient during early training, identifying samples with larger learning signal.

concepts.name: graph break

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A point where a compiler cannot capture part of a program and must fall back to eager execution, splitting optimized graph regions.

concepts.name: graphics processing unit (GPU)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A specialized processor originally designed for rendering graphics that provides massive parallel computing capabilities essential for efficient neural network computation, training, and inference.

concepts.name: Green AI

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A movement in AI research and practice that prioritizes computational efficiency and energy consumption as primary metrics alongside traditional performance metrics like accuracy.

concepts.name: Green500

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Ranking system that evaluates the world’s most powerful supercomputers based on energy efficiency measured in FLOP/s per watt rather than raw computational performance.

concepts.name: ground truth

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The reference target treated as correct for training or evaluation, often derived from measurement or annotation and therefore not necessarily identical to objective reality.

concepts.name: GRU

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Gated Recurrent Unit, a simplified variant of LSTM that uses fewer gates while maintaining the ability to capture long-term dependencies in sequential data.

concepts.name: hardware abstraction

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The layer in ML frameworks that provides a unified interface to diverse computing hardware (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, accelerators) while handling devicespecific optimizations and memory management behind the scenes.

concepts.name: hardware acceleration

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The use of specialized computing hardware to perform certain operations faster and more efficiently than software running on general-purpose processors.

concepts.name: hardware accelerator

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Specialized computing hardware designed to efficiently execute specific types of computations, such as GPUs for parallel processing or TPUs for machine learning workloads.

concepts.name: hardware-aware design

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The practice of designing neural network architectures specifically optimized for target hardware platforms, considering factors like memory hierarchy, compute units, and data movement patterns to maximize efficiency.

concepts.name: Hardware-software co-design

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 546; printed p. 529

concepts.definition: Hardware-Software Co-design is an ML accelerator development method that crosses conventional abstraction boundaries, allowing algorithm constraints to inform silicon design and hardware capabilities to shape algorithm formulation. 1...

concepts.name: hidden layer

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: An intermediate layer in a neural network between input and output layers that learns abstract representations by transforming data through learned weights and activation functions.

concepts.name: hidden state

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The internal memory of recurrent neural networks that carries information from previous time steps, enabling the network to maintain context across sequential inputs.

concepts.name: hierarchical processing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A multi-tier system architecture where data and intelligence flow between different levels of the computing stack, from sensors to edge devices to cloud systems.

concepts.name: high-bandwidth memory (HBM)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: An advanced memory technology that provides much higher bandwidth than traditional DRAM by using 3D stacking and wide interfaces, critical for data-intensive AI workloads.

concepts.name: horizontal scaling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Increasing system capacity by adding more machines or instances rather than upgrading existing hardware, providing better fault tolerance and load distribution.

concepts.name: hybrid machine learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The integration of multiple ML paradigms such as cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML to form unified distributed systems that combine complementary strengths.

concepts.name: Hybrid ML

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 97; printed p. 72

concepts.definition: Hybrid machine learning is the deployment strategy that distributes an ML pipeline across two or more deployment tiers, assigning each stage according to its latency, compute, data, and operational constraints. 1...

concepts.name: hybrid parallelism

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A distributed training approach that combines data parallelism and model parallelism to use the benefits of both strategies for training very large models.

concepts.name: hyperparameter

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A configuration setting that controls the learning process but is not learned from data, such as learning rate, batch size, or network architecture choices.

concepts.name: hyperscale data center

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Large-scale data center facilities containing thousands of servers and covering extensive floor space, designed to efficiently support massive computing workloads.

concepts.name: I/O bottleneck

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A performance limit where storage, decoding, preprocessing, or data transfer cannot supply data fast enough to keep compute resources busy.

concepts.name: idempotent transformation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A data transformation that has the same effect when applied repeatedly as when applied once, supporting safe retries and reprocessing.

concepts.name: im2col

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A convolution-lowering technique that unfolds image patches into matrix columns so convolution can execute as GEMM.

concepts.name: ImageNet

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A massive visual database containing over 14 million labeled images across 20,000+ categories, developed by a team led by Fei-Fei Li and introduced in 2009, whose annual challenge became instrumental in driving breakthrough advances in computer vision.

concepts.name: imperative

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: paradigm in which programs specify sequences of commands that update state and direct control flow; it is distinct from whether operations execute eagerly or are staged for later execution.

concepts.name: inductive bias

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A structural assumption built into a model or architecture that restricts the functions it can learn efficiently, such as locality in CNNs.

concepts.name: inference

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: The operational phase where trained neural networks make predictions on new data using fixed parameters, without weight updates.

concepts.name: InfiniBand

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A high-throughput, low-latency networking technology commonly used for

concepts.name: information-compute ratio (ICR)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A metric quantifying the efficiency of data selection, defined as the ratio of model performance gain to the computational cost (FLOPs) required to achieve it. Maximizing ICR is the primary goal of data selection strategies.

concepts.name: infrastructure as code

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Practice of managing and provisioning computing infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes, enabling version control and automation.

concepts.name: INT8

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: An 8-bit signed-integer representation used to quantize weights, activations, or both. Each INT8 value occupies one quarter the storage of an FP32 value, and supported hardware can accelerate applicable operations, with accuracy depending on the quantization scheme.

concepts.name: intermediate representation (IR)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A compilerinternal representation between frontend model code and backend hardware code generation, used by ML frameworks for optimization and portability.

concepts.name: internet of things

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies that connect and exchange data with other devices and systems over the internet.

concepts.name: intersectional analysis

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Evaluation that considers combinations of demographic attributes (for example, race and gender simultaneously) to detect concentrated harms not visible in single-factor analysis.

concepts.name: IOPS

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Input/Output Operations Per Second; a storage performance metric measuring the number of read/write operations a device can handle per second, critical for random access workloads like training data loading.

concepts.name: Iron Law of ML Systems

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A quantitative framework decomposing ML system performance into three terms: Data (limited by bandwidth), Compute (limited by FLOP/s), and Latency (limited by overhead). Formulated as T= Dvol/BW+O/(Rpeak ⋅ηhw)+Llat.

concepts.name: iterative pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A gradual pruning strategy that removes parameters in multiple stages with fine-tuning between each stage, allowing the model to adapt to reduced capacity and typically achieving better accuracy than one-shot pruning.

concepts.name: JAX

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A numerical computing library developed by Google Research that combines NumPy’s API with functional programming transformations including automatic differentiation, just-in-time compilation, and automatic vectorization for high-performance machine learning research.

concepts.name: JIT compilation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: Just-In-Time compilation that analyzes and optimizes code at runtime, enabling frameworks to balance the flexibility of eager execution with the performance benefits of graph optimization by compiling frequently used functions.

concepts.name: k-anonymity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A privacy technique that ensures each record in a dataset is indistinguishable from at least k-1 other records by generalizing quasi-identifiers.

concepts.name: kernel

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 926; printed p. 916

concepts.definition: A small matrix of learnable weights used in convolutional layers to detect specific features through the convolution operation, also called a filter. In GPU programming,

concepts.name: kernel fusion

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: An optimization technique that combines multiple computational operations into a single kernel to reduce memory transfers and improve performance on parallel processors.

concepts.name: keyword spotting (KWS)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A technology that detects specific wake words or phrases in audio streams, typically used in voice-activated devices with constraints on power consumption and latency.

concepts.name: knowledge distillation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A model compression technique where a smaller “student” network learns to mimic the behavior of a larger “teacher” network by training on the teacher’s soft output probabilities rather than just hard labels.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K-S test)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A nonparametric test that measures the maximum distance between two cumulative distributions, often used to compare feature distributions for drift.

concepts.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL divergence)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: An asymmetric information-theoretic measure of how one probability distribution differs from another, used in monitoring and drift analysis.

concepts.name: KV cache

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Stored key and value tensors from previous transformer tokens used during autoregressive inference to avoid recomputing attention history.

concepts.name: L0 norm

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The count of nonzero elements in a vector or tensor, used in pruning to express sparsity or a target budget for remaining weights.

concepts.name: label quality drift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Degradation in the reliability or consistency of labels over time, even when the underlying input distribution remains stable.

concepts.name: label shift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A distribution shift where label frequencies change while the feature patterns conditioned on labels remain stable.

concepts.name: LAPACK

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Linear Algebra Package that extends BLAS with higher-level linear algebra operations including matrix decompositions, eigenvalue problems, and linear system solutions, providing essential mathematical foundations for machine learning computations.

concepts.name: latency

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The time delay between a request or event and the corresponding response or completion, critical in real-time applications where prompt responses are required.

concepts.name: Latency budget

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 711; printed p. 696

concepts.definition: Latency budget is the time allocated to request stages under an end-to-end deadline; the SLO also specifies the required completion quantile. Significance: It acts as a zero-sum constraint system where any milliseconds consumed by serialization or network overhead directly reduce the latency budget (Llat) available for model inference.

concepts.name: latency constraints

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Real-time requirements that limit the maximum acceptable delay for model inference, driving optimization decisions in deployment scenarios where response time is critical.

concepts.name: layer normalization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A normalization technique that normalizes inputs across the features dimension for each sample, commonly used in transformer architectures to stabilize training.

concepts.name: layerwise quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A quantization granularity where all parameters within a single layer share the same quantization parameters, providing computational efficiency but potentially limiting representational precision compared to finer-grained approaches.

concepts.name: learning rate

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A hyperparameter that determines the step size for weight updates during gradient descent optimization, critically affecting training stability and convergence speed.

concepts.name: learning rate scheduling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The systematic adjustment of learning rates during training, using strategies like step decay, exponential decay,

concepts.name: lifecycle coherence

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The principle that all stages of ML development should align with overall system objectives, maintaining consistency in data handling, model architecture, and evaluation criteria.

concepts.name: linear scaling failure

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The phenomenon where increasing computing resources (for example, doubling accelerators) results in sublinear performance gains due to communication overhead and synchronization costs.

concepts.name: LINPACK

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Benchmark developed at Argonne National Laboratory that measures system performance by solving dense systems of linear equations, famous for its use in TOP500 supercomputer rankings.

concepts.name: Little’s Law

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A queuing relationship stating that average concurrency equals arrival rate times average time in the system, linking throughput, latency, and capacity.

concepts.name: Llama

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Large Language Model Meta AI, a family of open foundation models that popularized efficient architectural choices like RMSNorm and SwiGLU, serving as a modern reference point for large-scale transformer efficiency.

concepts.name: LLM performance metrics

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 738; printed p. 723

concepts.definition: LLM performance metrics separate initial responsiveness from the cadence of streaming autoregressive generation. Significance: They decompose user-perceived latency into time to first token (TTFT) (whose prefill work is often compute-bound) and time per output token (TPOT) (whose decode work is often bandwidth-bound at small batches).

concepts.name: load balancing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Distribution of incoming requests across multiple server instances to prevent bottlenecks, improve response times, and ensure high availability.

concepts.name: locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A hashing family that maps similar items to the same buckets with high probability, enabling scalable approximate similarity search.

concepts.name: logits

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The raw, unnormalized scores output by the last layer of a neural network before the activation function (like softmax) converts them into probabilities.

concepts.name: loss function

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A mathematical function that measures how well model outputs satisfy a training objective, providing the objective minimized by the training algorithm.

concepts.name: loss scaling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A technique used in mixedprecision training that multiplies the loss by a large factor before backpropagation to prevent gradient underflow in reduced precision formats.

concepts.name: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The theory that large neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that, when trained in isolation from proper initialization, can achieve comparable accuracy to the full network while being significantly smaller.

concepts.name: low-rank factorization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A matrix decomposition technique that approximates large weight matrices as products of smaller matrices, reducing the number of parameters and computational operations required for neural network layers.

concepts.name: LSTM

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Long Short-Term Memory, a type of recurrent neural network architecture designed to handle long-term dependencies through gating mechanisms that control information flow.

concepts.name: machine learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A subset of artificial intelligence that enables systems to automatically improve performance on tasks through experience and data rather than explicit programming.

concepts.name: Machine learning benchmarking

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 631; printed p. 614

concepts.definition: Machine learning benchmarking is the empirical measurement of ML workloads under specified conditions, used to test claims about components, models, or end-to-end systems against representative evidence rather than peak specifications alone.
