Significance: The gap between peak and sustained performance can be large.

concepts.name: machine learning framework

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A software platform that provides tools and abstractions for designing, training, and deploying machine learning models, bridging user applications with infrastructure through computational graphs, hardware optimization, and workflow orchestration. Examples include TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX.

concepts.name: Machine learning frameworks

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 310; printed p. 289

concepts.definition: Machine learning frameworks are software systems that translate high-level mathematical model definitions into hardware-optimized execution plans by managing the computational graph, automatic differentiation, kernel dispatch, and memory allocation across the hardware hierarchy. Significance: Frameworks directly determine the system efficiency (ηhw) term in the iron law.

concepts.name: machine learning lifecycle

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A structured, iterative process that encompasses all stages involved in developing, deploying, and maintaining machine learning systems, from problem definition through ongoing monitoring and improvement.

concepts.name: machine learning operations (MLOps)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The engineering discipline and set of tools focused on operationalizing machine learning models through automation, monitoring, and management of the entire ML pipeline from development to production.

concepts.name: Machine learning system benchmarks

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 639; printed p. 622

concepts.definition: Machine learning system benchmarks are standardized evaluation protocols that hold the workload and quality target constant while varying the hardware-software stack, measuring ηhw = Rsustained/Rpeak and Llat to isolate infrastructure efficiency from algorithmic improvements. 1. Significance: The same ResNet-50 model can deliver very different throughput across hardware stacks, precision formats, batch sizes, and compiler configurations, yet still report the same ImageNet Top-1 accuracy...

concepts.name: Machine learning systems

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 39; printed p. 12

concepts.definition: Machine learning systems are software systems whose core behavior is determined by parameters learned from data rather than explicitly programmed rules, making performance a function of data quality, algorithm choice, and hardware capacity simultaneously. Significance: Requirements are end to end.

concepts.name: machine learning systems engineering

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The engineering discipline focused on building reliable, efficient, and scalable AI systems across computational platforms, spanning the entire AI lifecycle from data acquisition through deployment and operations with emphasis on resource-awareness and system-level optimization.

concepts.name: macro benchmarks

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Evaluation methodology that assesses complete machine learning models to understand how architectural choices and component interactions affect overall system behavior and performance.

concepts.name: magnitude-based pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The most common pruning method that removes parameters with the smallest absolute values, based on the assumption that weights with smaller magnitudes contribute less to the model’s output.

concepts.name: Mapping in AI acceleration

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 595; printed p. 578

concepts.definition: Mapping in AI Acceleration is the accelerator-compiler process of binding the Logical Computation Graph to the Physical Hardware Topology by deciding which operations execute on which processing elements, which data resides in which memory tier, and in what temporal order. 1...

concepts.name: masking

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: An anonymization technique that alters or obfuscates sensitive values so they cannot be directly traced back to the original data subject.

concepts.name: membership inference attack

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A privacy attack that tries to determine whether a specific record was included in a model’s training data.

concepts.name: memory bandwidth

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Rate at which data can be read from or written to memory, measured in bytes per second, which often becomes a bottleneck in memory-intensive machine learning workloads.

concepts.name: memory hierarchy

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The organization of memory systems with different access speeds and capacities, from fast on-chip caches to slower off-chip main memory.

concepts.name: memory wall

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: The widening performance gap between processor speed and memory bandwidth, where computational capacity outpaces the rate at which data can be delivered to the processor, becoming a primary bottleneck for large ML models.

concepts.name: metadata

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Descriptive information about datasets that includes details about data collection, quality metrics, validation status, and other contextual information essential for data management.

concepts.name: micro benchmarks

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: Specialized evaluation tools that assess individual components or specific operations within machine learning systems, such as tensor operations or neural network layers.

concepts.name: micro-batch

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A smaller slice of an effective batch processed sequentially for gradient accumulation or pipeline parallelism to reduce peak memory.

concepts.name: microcontroller

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A small computer on a single integrated circuit containing a processor core, memory, and programmable input/output peripherals, commonly used in embedded systems.

concepts.name: MinHash

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A sketching method that approximates set similarity with compact signatures, commonly used for scalable nearduplicate detection.

concepts.name: mini-batch gradient descent

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 927; printed p. 917

concepts.definition: A training approach that computes gradients and updates weights using a small subset of training examples simultaneously, balancing compu-

concepts.name: mini-batch processing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: An optimization approach that computes gradients over small batches of examples, balancing the computational efficiency of batch processing with the memory constraints of stochastic methods.

concepts.name: mixed-precision computing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A technique that uses different numerical precisions at various stages of computation, such as FP16 for matrix multiplications and FP32 for accumulations.

concepts.name: mixed-precision training

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A training methodology that combines different numerical precisions (typically FP16 and FP32) to optimize memory usage and computational speed while maintaining training stability.

concepts.name: ML accelerator

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 554; printed p. 537

concepts.definition: Machine Learning Accelerators are processors or specialized units designed primarily for common neural-network tensor operations and dataflows. They pursue high Rpeak and data reuse on matching workloads by devoting more resources to arithmetic and local data movement than a general-purpose execution path can.

concepts.name: ML inference benchmarks

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 662; printed p. 645

concepts.definition: ML inference benchmarks are machine learning system benchmarks that quantify a system’s ability to meet latency constraints (Llat) at specified throughput levels, measuring scenariodefined latency statistics, throughput (queries per second), and power efficiency across representative serving scenarios. 1...

concepts.name: ML node

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A single production ML application treated as an operational unit, including data pipelines, feature computation, model training, serving infrastructure, and monitoring.

concepts.name: ML systems

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Integrated computing systems comprising three core components: data that guides algorithmic behavior, learning algorithms that extract patterns from data, and computing infrastructure that enables both training and inference processes.

concepts.name: ML systems spectrum

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The range of machine learning system deployments from cloudbased systems with abundant resources to tiny embedded devices with severe constraints, each requiring different optimization strategies and trade-offs.

concepts.name: ML Test Score

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A production-readiness rubric for ML systems that evaluates data, model, infrastructure, and monitoring tests.

concepts.name: ML training benchmarks

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 656; printed p. 639

concepts.definition: ML training benchmarks are machine learning system benchmarks that measure the time to reach a target quality metric (for example, a specified validation accuracy or loss threshold) on a fixed dataset and model, quantifying the rate of convergence per unit of resource. Significance: Training benchmarks reveal large gaps invisible to hardware specs.

concepts.name: MLCommons

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Organization that develops and maintains industry-standard benchmarks for machine learning systems, including the MLPerf suite for training and inference evaluation.

concepts.name: MLOps

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 755; printed p. 741

concepts.definition: Machine learning operations (MLOps) is the engineering practice of productionizing ML systems through CI/CD, workflow orchestration, reproducibility, versioning, collaboration, continuous training and evaluation, monitoring, and feedback loops. Significance: The cost of not closing this loop appears as stale predictions, delayed detection, and avoidable recovery work.

concepts.name: MLPerf

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Industry-standard benchmark suite that provides standardized tests for training and inference across various deep learning workloads, enabling fair comparisons of machine learning systems.

concepts.name: MLPerf execution scenarios

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Standard MLPerf inference traffic scenarios that model sequential, synchronized, server, batch, and interactive workloads with different latency and throughput requirements.

concepts.name: MLPerf Inference

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Benchmark framework that evaluates machine learning inference performance across different deployment environments, from cloud data centers to mobile devices and embedded systems.

concepts.name: MLPerf Mobile

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Specialized benchmark that extends MLPerf evaluation to smartphones and mobile devices, measuring latency and responsiveness under strict power and memory constraints.

concepts.name: MLPerf Power

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: An MLPerf methodology for measuring power and energy efficiency of ML workloads alongside performance.

concepts.name: MLPerf Tiny

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Benchmark designed for embedded and ultra-low-power AI systems such as IoT devices, wearables, and microcontrollers operating with minimal processing capabilities.

concepts.name: MLPerf Training

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Standardized benchmark that evaluates machine learning training performance by measuring time-to-accuracy, throughput, and resource utilization across different hardware platforms.

concepts.name: mobile machine learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The execution of machine learning models directly on portable, battery-powered devices like smartphones and tablets, enabling personalized and responsive applications.

concepts.name: Mobile ML

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 86; printed p. 61

concepts.definition: Mobile machine learning is the deployment paradigm bounded by thermal design power (TDP) and battery energy. Significance: It is constrained by the few-watt heat dissipation capacity of passive cooling, requiring architectures that prioritize sustained energy efficiency over peak throughput (Rpeak).

concepts.name: model cards

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A standardized format for documenting machine learning models, captur-

concepts.name: model compression

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Techniques used to reduce the size and computational requirements of machine learning models while seeking to preserve accuracy, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices.

concepts.name: model deployment

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The process of integrating trained machine learning models into production systems where they can make predictions on new data and provide value to end users.

concepts.name: model drift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The degradation of machine learning model performance over time due to changes in data patterns, user behavior, or environmental conditions that differ from the original training conditions.

concepts.name: model evaluation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The systematic assessment of machine learning model performance using various metrics and validation techniques to determine whether the model meets requirements and is ready for deployment.

concepts.name: model FLOPs utilization (MFU)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The ratio of the model FLOPs per second implied by observed throughput to the hardware’s theoretical peak FLOPs per second, measuring how effectively a workload uses available compute for model computation.

concepts.name: model optimization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The systematic refinement of machine learning models to enhance their efficiency while maintaining effectiveness, balancing trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, memory usage, latency, and energy efficiency.

concepts.name: model parallelism

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A distributed training strategy that splits a neural network model across multiple devices, with each device responsible for computing a portion of the network.

concepts.name: model quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The process of reducing numerical precision in machine learning models, typically from FP32 to INT8, to decrease model size and memory traffic; speed increases only with efficient low-precision kernels.

concepts.name: model registry

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Centralized repository for storing, versioning, and managing trained machine learning models with associated metadata, facilitating model governance and deployment.

concepts.name: model serving

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Infrastructure and systems that expose deployed machine learning models through APIs to handle prediction requests at scale with appropriate latency and throughput.

concepts.name: model training

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The process of using machine learning algorithms to learn patterns from training data, adjusting model parameters to minimize prediction errors and create a functional predictive system.

concepts.name: model validation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The process of testing machine learning models on independent datasets to assess their generalization ability and ensure they perform reliably on unseen data.

concepts.name: model versioning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The systematic tracking and management of different versions of machine learning models, including their parameters, training data, and performance metrics, to enable comparison and rollback capabilities.

concepts.name: model-centric AI

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A research paradigm where the dataset is treated as fixed and engineering effort focuses on optimizing model architecture.

concepts.name: momentum

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: An optimization technique that accumulates a velocity vector across iterations to help gradient descent navigate through local minima and accelerate convergence in consistent gradient directions.

concepts.name: monitoring

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The continuous observation and measurement of machine learning system

concepts.name: multi-head attention

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: An attention mechanism that uses multiple parallel attention heads, each focusing on different aspects of the input to capture diverse types of relationships simultaneously.

concepts.name: multilayer perceptron (MLP)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers between input and output layers, capable of learning nonlinear mappings through dense connections and activation functions.

concepts.name: Multilayer perceptrons

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 253; printed p. 231

concepts.definition: Multilayer perceptrons are feed-forward neural network architectures that apply fully connected layers in sequence, where every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next, encoding no structural assumption about the input domain. 1...

concepts.name: multiply-accumulate (MAC)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The operation of multiplying two values and accumulating the result into a running sum, dominating linear layers and accelerator datapaths.

concepts.name: MYCIN

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: One of the first large-scale expert systems developed at Stanford beginning in 1972 to diagnose blood infections, representing the shift toward capturing human expert knowledge in specific domains rather than pursuing general artificial intelligence.

concepts.name: N:M sparsity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A structured sparsity pattern where exactly N of every M values are nonzero, giving hardware more regular zero patterns to exploit.

concepts.name: neural architecture search

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: An automated approach that searches possible combinations of layers, connections, and architectural hyperparameters to find neural network architectures that perform well under specified objectives and constraints.

concepts.name: neural network

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A computational model consisting of interconnected nodes organized in layers that can learn to map inputs to outputs through adjustable connection weights.

concepts.name: neural processing unit (NPU)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Specialized processors designed specifically for accelerating neural network operations and machine learning computations, optimized for parallel processing of AI workloads.

concepts.name: neuromorphic computing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A computing approach that mimics the structure and function of biological neural networks, potentially offering more energy-efficient processing for AI applications.

concepts.name: NoSQL

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: A category of database systems designed to handle large volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data with flexible schemas, often used in big data applications.

concepts.name: numerical precision optimization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The dimension of model optimization that addresses how numerical values are represented and processed, including quantization techniques that map high-precision values to lower-bit representations.

concepts.name: NVLink

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth GPU interconnect for intra-node communication, useful for gradient synchronization and modelparallel activation transfers.

concepts.name: observability

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Comprehensive monitoring approach that provides insight into system behavior through metrics, logs, and traces, enabling understanding of internal states from external outputs.

concepts.name: on-chip memory

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: Fast memory integrated directly onto the processor chip, including caches and scratchpad memory, providing high bandwidth and low latency data access.

concepts.name: on-device learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 928; printed p. 918

concepts.definition: The capability for machine learning models to adapt and learn directly on edge devices without requiring data transmission to external servers.

concepts.name: one-hot encoding

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A representation where categorical labels become vectors with a single 1 and remaining 0s.

concepts.name: one-shot pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A pruning strategy where a large fraction of parameters is removed in a single step, typically followed by fine-tuning to recover accuracy, offering simplicity but potentially requiring more aggressive finetuning.

concepts.name: online inference

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Real-time prediction serving that processes individual requests with low latency, suitable for interactive applications requiring immediate responses.

concepts.name: ONNX

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Open Neural Network Exchange, a standardized format for representing machine learning models that enables interoperability between different frameworks, allowing models trained in one framework to be deployed using another.

concepts.name: ONNX Runtime

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Cross-platform inference engine that optimizes machine learning models through techniques like operator fusion and kernel tuning to improve inference speed and reduce computational overhead.

concepts.name: Operator fusion

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 525; printed p. 507

concepts.definition: Operator fusion is a compiler and runtime optimization that combines adjacent tensor operations into a single fused kernel so intermediate values remain in registers or on-chip memory instead of being written to and reread from accelerator global memory. 1...

concepts.name: optimizer

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: An algorithm that adjusts model parameters during training to minimize the loss function, with common examples including SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent), Adam, and RMSprop, each with different strategies for parameter updates.

concepts.name: optimizer state

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Auxiliary values maintained by an optimizer in addition to model parameters, such as Adam’s momentum and variance tensors, often dominating training memory for large models.

concepts.name: orchestration

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Coordination and management of complex workflows and distributed computing tasks, often using platforms like Kubernetes for container management.

concepts.name: outlier detection

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The process of identifying data points that significantly deviate from normal patterns, which may represent errors, anomalies, or valuable rare events.

concepts.name: overfitting

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A phenomenon where a model learns specific details of training data so well that it fails to generalize to new, unseen examples, typically indicated by high training accuracy but poor validation performance.

concepts.name: padding

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A technique in convolutional networks that adds zeros or other values around the input borders to control the spatial dimensions of the output feature maps.

concepts.name: PagedAttention

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A KV-cache memorymanagement technique that stores attention context in fixed-size pages rather than contiguous per-request blocks to reduce fragmentation.

concepts.name: paradigm shift

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A fundamental change in scientific approach, like the shift from symbolic reasoning to statistical learning in AI during the 1990s, and from shallow to deep learning in the 2010s, requiring researchers to abandon established methods for radically different approaches.

concepts.name: parallelism

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The simultaneous execution of multiple computational tasks or operations, fundamental to achieving high performance in neural network processing.

concepts.name: parameter

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A learnable component of a neural network, including weights and biases, that gets adjusted during training to minimize the loss function.

concepts.name: Pareto frontier

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The set of configurations where improving one objective requires worsening another, used to reason about accuracy, latency, memory, and energy trade-offs.

concepts.name: partitioning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A database technique that divides large datasets into smaller, manageable segments based on specific criteria to improve query performance and system scalability.

concepts.name: perceptron

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The fundamental building block of neural networks, consisting of weighted inputs, a bias term, and an activation function that produces a single output.

concepts.name: performance insights

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Analytical observations derived from monitoring production machine learning systems that reveal opportunities for improvement in model accuracy, system efficiency, or user experience.

concepts.name: performance-per-data (PPD)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A metric measuring the accuracy gain per training sample, used to evaluate the quality of a dataset or selection strategy. High PPD indicates a dataset rich in information and low in redundancy.

concepts.name: pinned memory

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Page-locked host memory that enables direct, asynchronous transfers between CPU and GPU, improving dataloading throughput at the cost of reserving system memory.

concepts.name: pipeline jungle

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Anti-pattern where complex, interdependent data processing pipelines become difficult to maintain, debug, and modify, leading to technical debt and operational complexity.

concepts.name: pipeline parallelism

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A form of model parallelism where different layers of a model are placed on different devices and data flows through them in a pipeline fashion, allowing multiple batches to be processed simultaneously.

concepts.name: point-in-time correctness

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The guarantee that training examples use only feature values that would have been available at the historical prediction time, preventing leakage.

concepts.name: pooling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A downsampling operation in convolutional networks that reduces spatial dimensions while retaining important features, commonly using max or average operations over local regions.

concepts.name: population stability index (PSI)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A binned distribution-shift metric that compares current feature distributions against a baseline to detect population drift.

concepts.name: positional encoding

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A method used in transformer architectures to inject information about the position of tokens in a sequence, since transformers lack inherent sequential processing.

concepts.name: post-training quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A quantization approach applied to already-trained models without modifying the training process, typically involving calibration on representative data to determine optimal quantization parameters.

concepts.name: power usage effectiveness (PUE)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Metric used in data centers to measure energy efficiency, calculated as the ratio of total facility power consumption to IT equipment power consumption.

concepts.name: power wall

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The technological barrier reached around 2005 where increasing processor frequency no longer yielded performance gains without unsustainable increases in power density and heat generation, forcing a shift to parallel and specialized architectures.

concepts.name: precision

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: In numerical computing, the number of significant bits or digits used to represent values, affecting computational accu-

concepts.name: prefetching

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A system optimization technique that loads data into memory before it is needed, overlapping data loading with computation to reduce idle time and improve training throughput.

concepts.name: problem definition

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The initial stage of machine learning development that involves clearly specifying objectives, constraints, success metrics, and operational requirements to guide all subsequent development decisions.

concepts.name: processing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: database approach optimized for complex analytical queries across large datasets, typically used in data warehouses for business intelligence.

concepts.name: processing element (PE)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A repeated accelerator building block containing compute units and local storage, with arrays of PEs providing parallel tensor execution.

concepts.name: programmable logic controller (PLC)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Industrial control systems used in manufacturing and IoT environments that can be integrated with ML models for automated decision-making in operational technology contexts.

concepts.name: protein folding problem

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The scientific challenge of predicting the three-dimensional structure and dynamics of proteins from their amino acid sequences and environments, a longstanding problem on which systems such as AlphaFold achieved breakthrough accuracy without resolving every folding question.

concepts.name: proxy variable

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A feature that indirectly carries signal about a protected or sensitive attribute even when that attribute is removed.

concepts.name: Pruning

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 486; printed p. 468

concepts.definition: Pruning is a model-compression technique that sparsifies the parameter space by removing weights that contribute minimal information to the loss landscape. Significance: It can convert dense matrices into sparse structures, reducing memory footprint and total data volume (Dvol) when the sparse representation, metadata, and recovery procedure preserve acceptable quality.

concepts.name: pseudonymization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A privacy technique that replaces direct identifiers with artificial identifiers while maintaining the ability to trace records for analysis purposes.

concepts.name: PyTorch

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A deep learning framework developed by Facebook’s AI Research lab that emphasizes dynamic computational graphs, eager execution, and intuitive Python integration, particularly popular for research and experimentation.

concepts.name: quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A model-compression technique that represents parameters or activations at lower precision, such as FP32 to INT8, reducing storage and data movement without reducing mathematical operation count; speedups require supported hardware and kernels.

concepts.name: quantization granularity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The level at which quantization parameters are applied, ranging from per-tensor (coarsest) to per-channel or per-group (finer), with finer granularity typically preserving more accuracy but requiring more storage.

concepts.name: quantization-aware training

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: A training approach where quantization effects are simulated during the training process, allowing the model to adapt to reduced precision and typically achieving better accuracy than post-training quantization.

concepts.name: queries per second (QPS)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Performance metric that measures how many inference requests a system can process in one second, commonly used to evaluate throughput in production deployments.

concepts.name: query-key-value

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: The three components of attention mechanisms where queries determine what to look for, keys represent what is available, and values contain the actual information to be weighted and combined.

concepts.name: real-time processing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 929; printed p. 919

concepts.definition: Processing data as it becomes available under application timing

concepts.name: receptive field

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The region of the input that influences a particular neuron’s output, determining the spatial extent of patterns that can be detected by that neuron.

concepts.name: recurrent neural network

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A type of neural network designed for sequential data processing, featuring connections that create loops allowing information to persist across time steps.

concepts.name: Recurrent neural networks

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 268; printed p. 246

concepts.definition: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are sequence-processing architectures that maintain a hidden state ht= f(ht−1,xt) updated at each time step, encoding the assumption that the current output depends on all prior inputs through this fixed-size state vector. 1...

concepts.name: Red AI

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: AI research and development that prioritizes maximizing accuracy or performance without regard for the increasing computational and environmental costs required.

concepts.name: regularization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Techniques used to prevent overfitting in neural networks by adding constraints or penalties, including methods like dropout, weight decay, and data augmentation.

concepts.name: ReLU

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Rectified Linear Unit activation function defined as f(x) = max(0,x) that introduces nonlinearity while maintaining computational efficiency and helping mitigate vanishing gradients for positive inputs.

concepts.name: residual connection

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A skip connection that adds the input of a layer to its output, enabling the training of very deep networks by mitigating the vanishing gradient problem.

concepts.name: ResNet

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Residual Network, a deep convolutional architecture built from residual blocks with skip connections, enabling the training of networks with hundreds of layers and achieving breakthrough performance.

concepts.name: ResNet-50

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A specific 50-layer variant of the Residual Network architecture that serves as the canonical lighthouse model for computebound workloads, balancing depth and computational cost for vision benchmarks.

concepts.name: Responsible AI engineering

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 825; printed p. 812

concepts.definition: Responsible AI engineering is the engineering discipline of designing, deploying, and maintaining systems with probabilistic outputs by operationalizing societal and regulatory requirements as testable constraints on the D·A·M axes: permissible data contents, provenance, and composition; allowable model behavior and robustness properties; and infrastructure bounds such as latency, energy, compute budget, carbon emissions, and audit-log retention. 1...

concepts.name: retinal fundus photographs

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Medical images of the interior surface of the eye, including the retina, optic disc, and blood vessels, commonly used for diagnosing eye diseases and training medical AI systems.

concepts.name: reverse-mode differentiation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An automatic differentiation technique that computes gradients by traversing the computational graph in reverse order, highly efficient for functions with many inputs and few outputs, making it ideal for neural network training.

concepts.name: ridge point

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The arithmetic intensity at which a workload transitions from memory-bound to compute bound on a given hardware platform, calculated as peak FLOP/s divided by memory bandwidth. The inflection point on the Roofline Model diagram.

concepts.name: Ring AllReduce

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A bandwidth-efficient AllReduce algorithm where devices pass chunks around a ring and accumulate results for distributed gradient synchronization.

concepts.name: RMSprop

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm that maintains a moving average of squared gradients to automatically adjust learning rates for each parameter during training.

concepts.name: role-based access control (RBAC)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An accesscontrol model that grants permissions according to user, service, or team roles rather than ad hoc individual grants.

concepts.name: rollback

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Process of reverting to a previous stable version of a model or system when issues are detected in production, ensuring service continuity.

concepts.name: roofline analysis

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A performance modeling technique that plots attainable performance against operational intensity, with peak compute and bandwidth forming the ceilings, to identify whether a system is memory bound or compute bound.

concepts.name: scalability

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The ability of machine learning systems to handle increasing amounts of data, users, or computational demands without significant degradation in performance or user experience.

concepts.name: scale and zero-point

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Quantization parameters that map real-valued tensors to integer values and back, where scale controls step size and zero-point maps real zero into the quantized range.

concepts.name: schema

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The structure and format definition of data that specifies data types, field names, and relationships, essential for data validation and processing consistency.

concepts.name: schema evolution

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The process of modifying data schemas over time while maintaining backward compatibility and ensuring continued functionality of dependent systems and applications.

concepts.name: schema-on-read

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An approach used in data lakes where data structure is defined and enforced at the time of reading rather than when storing, providing flexibility for diverse data types.

concepts.name: scratchpad memory

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Fast software-managed local memory used by accelerators to stage predictable data movement under compiler or runtime control.

concepts.name: segmentation maps

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Detailed annotations that classify objects at the pixel level, providing the most granular labeling information but requiring significantly more storage and processing resources.

concepts.name: self-attention

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An attention mechanism where queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence, allowing each position to attend to all positions including itself.

concepts.name: semi-supervised learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A machine learning approach that uses both labeled and unlabeled data for training, using structural assumptions to improve model performance with limited labels.

concepts.name: sensitivity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The proportion of actual positive cases correctly identified by a classification model, also known as true positive rate or recall; critical in medical applications where missing positive cases has severe consequences.

concepts.name: serverless

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Cloud computing model where infrastructure is automatically managed by the provider, allowing code execution without server management concerns.

concepts.name: service level agreement (SLA)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A formal external contract specifying service commitments, often through one or more SLOs, and the consequences or penalties for noncompliance.

concepts.name: service-level objective (SLO)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An internal measurable target for a service-level indicator such as latency, error rate, or availability that guides operations and may underpin an external SLA.

concepts.name: shadow deployment

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A deployment strategy where a new model runs in parallel with the production model, making predictions that are logged but not served to users, enabling validation without user impact.

concepts.name: shallow learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Machine learning approaches that use algorithms with limited complexity, such as support vector machines and decision trees, which require carefully engineered features but cannot automatically discover hierarchical representations like deep learning methods.

concepts.name: SHAP values

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Feature-attribution scores based on Shapley values that estimate each feature’s contribution to a model prediction.

concepts.name: sigmoid

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An activation function that maps input values to a range between 0 and 1, histori-

concepts.name: silent bias

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Model unfairness that produces valid-looking but discriminatory outputs, evading traditional error monitoring and requiring disaggregated evaluation to detect.

concepts.name: silent degradation

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The gradual decline in ML system performance that occurs without triggering errors, exceptions, or alerts. An ML system can continue operating while producing increasingly inaccurate predictions.

concepts.name: silent failure

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A system failure mode where an ML model continues to produce plausiblelooking outputs that are gradually less accurate or contextually relevant without triggering conventional error alerts.

concepts.name: SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A parallel computing architecture that applies the same operation to multiple data elements simultaneously, effective for regular data-parallel computations.

concepts.name: SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An extension of SIMD that enables parallel execution across multiple independent threads, each maintaining its own state and program counter.

concepts.name: singular value decomposition

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A matrix factorization technique that decomposes a matrix into the product of three matrices, commonly used in low-rank approximations to compress neural network layers by retaining only the most significant singular values.

concepts.name: skip connection

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A direct connection that bypasses one or more layers, allowing gradients to flow more easily through deep networks and enabling better training of very deep architectures.

concepts.name: SLOs and SLAs

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 665; printed p. 648

concepts.definition: SLOs and SLAs are performance commitment specifications for production ML serving systems: a service-level objective (SLO) is a target value or range for a service-level indicator, while an SLA is a contract that specifies service objectives and the consequences of failing to meet them. 1...

concepts.name: soft targets

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Teacher-model probability distributions used as supervision in knowledge distillation, carrying class-similarity information beyond hard labels.

concepts.name: softmax

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An activation function that converts logits into a probability distribution where outputs sum to 1, used in multi-class classification.

concepts.name: sparse Tensor Core

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: A Tensor Core variant that accelerates supported structured sparsity patterns such as 2:4 sparsity by skipping constrained zero values.

concepts.name: sparsity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The property of tensors in which many values are exactly zero, which can improve computational efficiency when the zeros have suitable structure and specialized sparse kernels or hardware support them; near-zero values count only after pruning.

concepts.name: SPEC CPU

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Standardized benchmark suite developed by the System Performance Evaluation Cooperative that measures processor performance using real-world applications rather than synthetic tests.

concepts.name: special function unit (SFU)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Dedicated hardware for specialized operations such as exponentials, reciprocals, roots, and some activation-function primitives that do not map cleanly to ordinary arithmetic or matrix multiply units.

concepts.name: specificity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: The proportion of actual negative cases correctly identified by a classification model, also known as true negative rate; important for avoiding overwhelming referral systems with false positives.

concepts.name: SPECpower

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: Benchmark methodology that measures server energy efficiency across varying workload levels, enabling direct comparisons of power-performance trade-offs in computing systems.

concepts.name: speculative decoding

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 930; printed p. 920

concepts.definition: An optimization technique for autoregressive language models where a smaller model generates draft tokens that are then verified by a larger model,

concepts.name: speed of light (latency)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The physical speed limit of information transmission (approx. 200,000 km/s in fiber), creating an irreducible lower bound on network latency that necessitates edge computing for applications requiring sub-10 ms response times over long distances.

concepts.name: state dict

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A framework serialization mapping from module or optimizer names to tensors, used to save, load, and checkpoint models and optimizer state.

concepts.name: static graph

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A computational graph that is defined completely before execution begins, enabling comprehensive optimization and efficient deployment but requiring all operations to be specified upfront, limiting runtime flexibility.

concepts.name: static quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A quantization approach where quantization parameters are determined once during calibration and remain fixed during inference, providing computational efficiency but less adaptability than dynamic approaches.

concepts.name: statistical learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The era of machine learning that emerged in the 1990s, shifting focus from rule-based symbolic AI to algorithms that could learn patterns from data, laying the groundwork for modern data-driven approaches to artificial intelligence.

concepts.name: stochastic gradient descent

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A variant of gradient descent that estimates gradients using individual training examples or small batches rather than the entire dataset, reducing memory requirements and enabling online learning.

concepts.name: Straight-Through Estimator (STE)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A gradient approximation that lets training pass gradients through nondifferentiable operations such as rounding, often used in quantization-aware training.

concepts.name: stream ingestion

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A data processing pattern that handles data in real-time as it arrives, essential for applications requiring immediate processing and low-latency responses.

concepts.name: stream processing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Real-time data processing approach that handles continuous flows of data as it arrives, enabling immediate responses to events and pattern detection.

concepts.name: stride

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The step size by which a convolutional filter moves across the input, controlling the spatial dimensions of the output and the degree of overlap between filter applications.

concepts.name: structured pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A pruning approach that removes entire computational units such as neurons, channels, or layers, producing smaller dense models that are more hardware-friendly than the sparse matrices created by unstructured pruning.

concepts.name: supervised learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A machine learning approach where models learn from labeled training examples to make predictions on new, unlabeled data.

concepts.name: symbolic AI

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: An approach to artificial intelligence that uses high-level symbolic representations of problems, logic, and search algorithms, dominant before the deep learning revolution and characterized by expert systems and rule-based reasoning.

concepts.name: synthetic benchmark

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Artificial test program designed to measure specific aspects of system performance, as opposed to benchmarks based on real-world applications and workloads.

concepts.name: synthetic data

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Artificially generated data created using algorithms, simulations, or generative models to supplement real-world datasets, addressing limitations in data availability or privacy concerns.

concepts.name: system entropy

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The tendency of ML systems to degrade over time as the world changes

concepts.name: System-on-Chip (SoC)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: An integrated circuit that incorporates most or all components of a computer or electronic system, including CPU, GPU, memory, and specialized processors on a single chip. Commonly used in mobile devices and embedded systems for space and power efficiency.

concepts.name: systems co-design

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Joint design of algorithms, software, and hardware so model structure and execution fit physical capabilities and constraints.

concepts.name: systems integration

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The process of combining various components and subsystems into a unified, functional system that operates efficiently and reliably as a whole.

concepts.name: systems thinking

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: An approach to understanding complex systems by considering how individual components interact and affect the whole system, particularly important in ML where data, algorithms, hardware, and deployment environments must work together effectively.

concepts.name: systolic array

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A specialized hardware architecture that efficiently performs matrix operations by streaming data through a grid of processing elements, minimizing data movement and energy consumption.

concepts.name: tail latency

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: High-percentile response time in a system, typically measured as P95 or P99 latency, important for characterizing slow requests under peak load but not equivalent to the absolute worst case. It complements median and mean latency rather than replacing them.

concepts.name: tailored inference benchmarks

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Specialized performance tests designed for specific deployment environments or use cases, accounting for unique constraints and optimization requirements.

concepts.name: tanh

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Hyperbolic tangent activation function that maps inputs to (-1, 1), providing zerocentered outputs.

concepts.name: technical debt

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Long-term maintenance cost accumulated from expedient design decisions during development, particularly problematic in ML systems due to data dependencies and model complexity.

concepts.name: Technical debt in ML

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 760; printed p. 746

concepts.definition: Technical debt in machine learning is the accumulating maintenance and change cost created by implicit data dependencies, entangled features, and undeclared consumers in ML systems, where the resulting liabilities may also appear as silent accuracy degradation. 1...

concepts.name: telemetry

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Automated collection and transmission of performance data and metrics from distributed systems, enabling remote monitoring and analysis.

concepts.name: tensor

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A multi-dimensional array used to represent data in neural networks, generalizing scalars (0D), vectors (1D), and matrices (2D) to higher dimensions.

concepts.name: Tensor Core

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A specialized GPU matrix unit for accelerated mixed-precision multiplyaccumulate operations on tensor tiles.

concepts.name: tensor decomposition

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The extension of matrix factorization to higher-order tensors, used to compress neural network layers by representing weight tensors as combinations of smaller tensors with fewer parameters.

concepts.name: tensor parallelism

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A model parallelism strategy where individual tensor operations (like matrix multiplication) are split across multiple devices, reducing memory per device and potentially reducing large-layer latency when the reduction in computation time exceeds the added communication time.

concepts.name: tensor processing unit (TPU)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Google’s custom application-specific integrated circuit designed specifically for machine learning workloads, optimized for matrix operations and featuring systolic array architecture.

concepts.name: TensorFlow

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A comprehensive machine learning framework developed by Google that provides tools for the entire ML pipeline from research to production, featuring both eager execution and graph-based computation with extensive ecosystem support.

concepts.name: TensorRT

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: NVIDIA’s inference optimization library that applies techniques like operator fusion and precision reduction to accelerate deep learning inference on GPU hardware.

concepts.name: ternarization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: An extreme quantization technique that constrains weights to three values (typically -1, 0, +1), providing significant compression while maintaining more representational capacity than binary quantization.

concepts.name: The consistency imperative

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 161; printed p. 136

concepts.definition: The Consistency Imperative requires equivalent transformation behavior and state across training and serving environments. Significance: KL divergence (DKL(pgserve‖pgtrain)) between feature distributions induced by the serving transformation gserve (current) and training transformation gtrain (baseline) can signal misalignment.

concepts.name: The constraint propagation principle

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 127; printed p. 102

concepts.definition: The constraint propagation principle states that a constraint discovered late in the ML lifecycle can force rework in affected earlier stages. Actual correction cost depends on which artifacts and decisions must change. This chapter’s 2Nstage−1 rule is an illustrative sensitivity scenario, not an empirical cost law.

concepts.name: The data locality invariant

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 83; printed p. 58

concepts.definition: The data locality invariant first tests a complete remote path against the service deadline. Let Tremote denote complete remote-path time, Tdeadline the deadline, BWnetwork offload bandwidth, Llat,network network latency, and Rpeak,remote and ηhw,remote the remote compute rate and efficiency: Tremote = Dvol BWnetwork +Llat,network+ O Rpeak,remote ⋅ηhw,remote , remote feasible ⟺Tremote ≤Tdeadline The corresponding Tlocal is the complete local-path time...

concepts.name: The D·A·M taxonomy

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 40; printed p. 13

concepts.definition: D·A·M taxonomy is a diagnostic framework that classifies any machine learning system performance bottleneck along three axes. Data determines what examples and bytes the system must process, Algorithm determines the model structure and work required to learn or predict, and Machine determines the hardware capacity available to execute that work.

concepts.name: The iron law of training performance

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 374; printed p. 354

concepts.definition: The iron law of training performance expresses training time through the workload’s operation count and its effective achieved throughput: Ttrain = O Rpeak ×ηhw (8.1) Here ηhw is an effective end-to-end utilization factor, the achieved model-operation rate divided by the relevant hardware peak. Data stalls, communication, synchronization, launch overhead, and inefficient kernels all reduce this factor...

concepts.name: thermal design power (TDP)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The sustained power and heat level a device or cooling system is designed to dissipate under typical maximum workload.

concepts.name: thermal throttling

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A protective mechanism in mobile and embedded devices that reduces processor clock speed and performance to prevent overheating, often limiting the sustained performance of on-device ML inference.

concepts.name: throughput

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The rate at which a system can process data or complete operations, typically measured in operations per second and crucial for training large models.

concepts.name: time per output token (TPOT)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The per-token latency during autoregressive decode after the first token, reflecting decode throughput and memory-bandwidth limits.

concepts.name: time to first token (TTFT)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The time from request arrival to the first generated token in streaming LLM serving, including prefill, scheduling, and initial response latency.

concepts.name: time-to-accuracy

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The wall-clock time required to train a model to a specified validation accuracy.

concepts.name: TinyML

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A field focused on deploying machine learning models on ultra-constrained embedded devices such as microcontrollers and sensors, operating in the milliwatt to subwatt power range, with severe limitations on memory, power, and computational capacity. Also called tiny machine learning.

concepts.name: TOPS

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: Tera Operations Per Second, an operation-rate unit indicating how many trillion operations a system can execute in one second. It is commonly reported for low-precision integer workloads, so the operation type and precision must be specified.

concepts.name: total cost of ownership (TCO)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A comprehensive financial metric for ML systems encompassing training, inference, and operational costs over the system’s entire lifecycle.

concepts.name: train-serve split

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A hybrid architecture pattern where computationally intensive model training occurs on powerful cloud infrastructure, while the trained model is optimized and deployed for inference on resource-constrained edge or mobile devices.

concepts.name: training

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: The process of adjusting neural network parameters using data or interaction experience and an optimization procedure to minimize a loss or maximize a reward.

concepts.name: Training systems

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 372; printed p. 352

concepts.definition: Machine learning training systems are software-hardware systems that execute the iterative optimization loop (forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, and parameter update) to minimize a loss function over a training dataset. 1...

concepts.name: training-serving skew

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A mismatch between how features or data are computed during model training vs. serving in production, which can degrade model performance. Common causes include different preprocessing pipelines, feature computation timing, or data sources between training and inference.

concepts.name: transfer learning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 931; printed p. 921

concepts.definition: A machine learning technique that uses knowledge gained from pretrained models on related tasks, allowing faster training and better performance on new

concepts.name: transformer

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A neural network architecture built from attention, feed-forward blocks, residual connections, and normalization; the original design eliminates recurrence and convolution, though later variants may incorporate them.

concepts.name: Transformers

source_location.raw: definition_box, PDF p. 278; printed p. 256

concepts.definition: Transformers are neural network architectures that combine self-attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections, normalization, and positional information without recurrence, enabling parallel processing across sequence positions during training and prefill. Significance: Parallelism is the systems payoff. An RNN processing an S-token sequence executes Sdependent steps.

concepts.name: translation equivariance

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A property where shifting the input causes a corresponding shift in the output feature map, distinct from invariance which discards position.

concepts.name: translation invariance

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The property that a model’s output remains unchanged when the input shifts. Convolution is translationequivariant; pooling or global aggregation can produce approximate invariance.

concepts.name: Tucker decomposition

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A tensor decomposition method that generalizes singular value decomposition to higher-order tensors using a core tensor and factor matrices, commonly used for compressing convolutional neural network layers.

concepts.name: TV white spaces

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: Unused broadcasting frequencies that can be repurposed for internet connectivity, as employed by systems like Farm- Beats to extend network access to remote agricultural sensors and IoT devices.

concepts.name: uniform quantization

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A quantization approach where the range of values is divided into evenly spaced intervals, providing simple implementation but potentially suboptimal for nonuniform value distributions.

concepts.name: universal approximation theorem

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A theoretical result proving that neural networks with sufficient width and a suitable nonlinear activation function can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to arbitrary accuracy.

concepts.name: unreasonable effectiveness of data

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The empirical observation that for many problems, adding more data is more effective than improving algorithms, driving the data-centric AI paradigm.

concepts.name: unstructured pruning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A pruning approach that removes individual weights while preserving the overall network architecture, creating sparse weight matrices that require specialized hardware support to realize computational benefits.

concepts.name: unstructured sparsity

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A form of model sparsity where individual weights are set to zero without following any particular pattern, creating irregular sparsity patterns that require specialized hardware support to realize computational benefits.

concepts.name: validation issues

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: Problems identified during model testing that indicate poor performance, overfitting, data quality problems, or other issues that must be resolved before deployment.

concepts.name: vanishing gradient problem

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A problem in deep neural networks where gradients become exponentially smaller as they propagate backward through layers, making it difficult for early layers to learn effectively.

concepts.name: vector operations

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: Computational operations that process multiple data elements simultaneously, enabling efficient parallel execution of element-wise transformations in neural networks.

concepts.name: verification gap

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The mismatch between finite test-set coverage and the much larger input space an ML system may encounter in production.

concepts.name: versioning

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The practice of tracking changes to datasets, models, and pipelines over time, enabling reproducibility, rollback capabilities, and audit trails in ML systems.

concepts.name: virtuous cycle

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The self-reinforcing process in deep learning where improvements in data availability, algorithms, and computing power each enable further advances in the other areas, accelerating overall progress.

concepts.name: Von Neumann bottleneck

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The performance limitation caused by the shared bus between processor and memory in traditional computer architectures, where data movement becomes more expensive than computation.

concepts.name: warehouse-scale computer (WSC)

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A data center operated as a single programmable computer, treating compute, storage, networking, and failures as system-level resources.

concepts.name: warp

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A group of 32 threads on NVIDIA GPUs whose active threads execute one common instruction at a time; the fundamental unit of thread scheduling on NVIDIA GPUs.

concepts.name: Waymo

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. that represents a leading deployment of machine learning systems in autonomous vehicle technology, demonstrating how ML systems can span from embedded systems to cloud infrastructure in safety-critical environments.

concepts.name: weak supervision

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: An approach that uses lowerquality labels obtained more efficiently through heuristics, distant supervision, or programmatic methods rather than manual expert annotation.

concepts.name: web scraping

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: An automated technique for extracting data from websites to build custom datasets, requiring careful consideration of legal, ethical, and technical constraints.

concepts.name: weight

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: A learnable parameter that determines the strength of connection between neurons in different layers, adjusted during training to minimize the loss function.

concepts.name: weight matrix

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: An organized collection of weights connecting one layer to another in a neural network, enabling efficient computation through matrix operations.

concepts.name: weight sharing

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: The practice of using the same parameters across different spatial locations, as in convolutional networks, reducing the number of parameters while maintaining pattern detection capabilities.

concepts.name: Whetstone

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: Early benchmark developed at the UK National Physical Laboratory by Curnow and Wichmann, first published as an ALGOL 60 program in 1972 and later as the canonical FORTRAN version in 1976. It measured floating-point arithmetic performance in MWIPS (millions of Whetstone instructions per second), becoming one of the first widely-adopted standardized performance tests.

concepts.name: workflow orchestration

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: Automated coordination and management of complex ML pipeline sequences, ensuring proper execution order, dependency management, and error handling across distributed systems.

concepts.name: XLA

source_location.raw: glossary, PDF p. 932; printed p. 922

concepts.definition: Accelerated Linear Algebra, a domainspecific compiler for linear algebra operations that optimizes TensorFlow and JAX computations by generating efficient code for various hardware platforms including CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs.
